summary: This standards-track RFC describes using the ChaCha stream cipher and Poly1305 authenticator in TLS and DTLS, defining cipher suites that use them. It updates RFCs 5246 and 6347.

eli5.summary: A different lock-and-seal combination for secure connections, helpful on devices that lack fast special hardware.

why use chacha20 instead of aes gcm
subtitle: Two fast, software-friendly primitives, ChaCha20 and Poly1305, become a new family of cipher suites for TLS and DTLS.

tldr.problem: CBC-mode cipher suites and the RC4 stream cipher in TLS and DTLS had known attack problems, and the existing AES-GCM suites raised concerns about performance and ease of software implementation.
tldr.mechanism: The document defines seven cipher suites built on the AEAD_CHACHA20_POLY1305 algorithm, with a 96-bit nonce formed from the record sequence number and the write IV, so no explicit per-record nonce is sent.
tldr.outcome: TLS 1.2 and DTLS 1.2 gain a stream-cipher option that is meant to be comparable to RC4 in speed and easy to implement without software side-channel weaknesses. RFC 7905 is itself updated by RFC 10015.

today: RFC 7905 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 5246 and RFC 6347. It is itself updated by RFC 10015, and no RFC obsoletes it.

sections.title: Why a New Cipher for TLS
sections.content:
RFC 7905 describes how to use the ChaCha stream cipher and the Poly1305 authenticator in version 1.2 or later of TLS (RFC 5246) and of DTLS (RFC 6347).

The text points to recent attacks on the CBC-mode cipher suites and on RC4, the only stream cipher TLS supported at the time. The existing AEAD suites based on AES-GCM fix some of these issues, but there are concerns about their performance and ease of software implementation. The goal is a stream cipher for both TLS and DTLS that is comparable to RC4 in speed on a wide range of platforms and can be implemented easily without being vulnerable to software side-channel attacks.
sections.eli5: The old locks on private connections had been picked by clever attackers, and the newer lock was slow on some devices. So people wanted a lock that is hard to pick and quick everywhere.

sections.title: ChaCha20 and Poly1305
sections.content:
ChaCha was developed by D. J. Bernstein in 2008 and is a refinement of Salsa20. The variant used here has 20 rounds, a 96-bit nonce and a 256-bit key, and is called ChaCha20. It is described in RFC 7539.

Poly1305 is a one-time authenticator. It takes a 256-bit one-time key and a message and produces a 16-byte tag, so that an attacker has a negligible chance of producing a valid tag for an inauthentic message.

Both were designed for high performance in software. They typically admit a compact implementation using few resources and inexpensive operations, and they are designed to minimize leakage of information through side-channels.
sections.eli5: ChaCha20 scrambles the message so nobody can read it. Poly1305 adds a small stamp that shows nobody changed it on the way.

sections.title: How the AEAD Fits into TLS
sections.content:
ChaCha20 and Poly1305 are combined into an AEAD algorithm, AEAD_CHACHA20_POLY1305, as described in RFC 7539 and the interface of RFC 5116. It plugs into TLS and DTLS the way Section 6.2.3.3 of RFC 5246 specifies.

The algorithm needs a 96-bit nonce, built in two steps. First, the 64-bit record sequence number is written as an 8-byte big-endian value and padded on the left with four 0x00 bytes. Second, that padded value is XORed with the client_write_IV (when the client sends) or the server_write_IV (when the server sends). In DTLS the 64-bit number is the 16-bit epoch followed by the 48-bit sequence number.

This differs from the AES-GCM nonce in TLS 1.2 but matches the scheme expected for TLS 1.3. Because both sides already know the sequence number and the shared secret, no explicit per-record nonce is sent. That saves eight bytes per record and stops implementations from wrongly using a random nonce. In RFC 5246 terms, fixed_iv_length is twelve bytes and record_iv_length is zero bytes.
sections.eli5: Each message gets a one-of-a-kind number made by mixing its place in line with a secret both sides share. Since both sides can work it out, nobody has to send it along.

sections.title: The Seven Cipher Suites
sections.content:
Seven cipher suites are defined, all with the code prefix 0xCC. Three use certificate-based key exchange and four use pre-shared keys. The key exchanges themselves are unchanged and are performed as defined in RFC 5246, RFC 4492 and RFC 5489.

For every suite, the pseudorandom function is the TLS PRF with SHA-256 as the hash function. Section 3 of the RFC says IANA added the same seven entries to the TLS Cipher Suite Registry.
sections.eli5: It is a menu of seven combinations. Each one says how the two sides first agree on a secret, and all of them then use the same scrambling and stamping recipe.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The text notes that ChaCha20 follows the same principle as Salsa20, a cipher with significant security review. At the time of writing there were no known significant security problems with either cipher. ChaCha20 is also the core of the BLAKE hash function, a SHA-3 finalist.

Poly1305 rejects forged messages with a probability of 1-(n/2^107), where n is the maximum input length. For TLS and DTLS this gives a maximum forgery probability of about 1 in 2^93.

These suites require that a nonce is never repeated under the same key. The design guarantees this by using the TLS sequence number, which is unique and does not wrap.

AEADs such as this one are not intended to hide the lengths of plaintexts. Traffic analysis is outside the scope of the AEAD, and the text says it is being addressed in future versions of TLS.
sections.eli5: The recipe has been studied by many experts without finding serious holes. It keeps the message secret but not how long the message is.
